title: Symmetric Key Cryptography
body:
**One key, shared in advance, used for both directions.** Alice encrypts with $k$, Bob decrypts
with the same $k$, and anyone holding $k$ can do both:

$$D_k(E_k(m)) = m$$

Every cipher in [[Classical Ciphers]] is symmetric, and so is everything anyone actually encrypts
bulk data with today. It is fast, it is well understood, and it has exactly one problem, which the
whole second half of the course exists to solve.

## The key distribution problem

To talk securely to someone you must already have shared a secret with them, over a channel that
was already secure. That is circular, and at scale it is fatal:

- $n$ people who all need to talk pairwise need $\binom{n}{2}$ distinct keys. Ten people is 45
  keys; a thousand is nearly half a million. That is [[Combination]] from [[DISCRETE MATH]] costing
  real money.
- The keys must be distributed **before** any communication happens, by courier or meeting, and
  re-distributed whenever anyone joins, leaves, or is compromised.
- You cannot open an encrypted connection to a stranger at all, which is the case the web is made
  of.

[[Public Key Cryptography]] solves exactly this and nothing else. It does not replace symmetric
cryptography; it delivers a symmetric key. **Every TLS connection is a public-key handshake
agreeing on an [[AES]] key, followed by symmetric encryption for the rest of the session**, because
public-key operations are orders of magnitude slower and nobody wants to do modular exponentiation
on a video stream.

## Stream versus block

The two shapes a modern symmetric cipher comes in.

| | [[Stream Cipher]] | Block cipher |
|---|---|---|
| Unit | one bit or byte at a time | fixed-size block (64 or 128 bits) |
| How | XOR plaintext with a keystream | keyed permutation of the block |
| State | keeps evolving internal state | stateless per block |
| Examples | RC4, LFSR-based, ChaCha20 | DES ([[Feistel Network]]), [[AES]] |
| Needs | never reuse a keystream | a [[Modes of Operation\|mode]] to handle >1 block |

A block cipher is a **[[Permutation]] of the block space chosen by the key**: with a 128-bit block
it picks one bijection on $\{0,1\}^{128}$ out of $2^{128}!$ possible ones, and the key names which.
It has to be a bijection or decryption is impossible, the same injectivity requirement the affine
cipher's $\gcd(a,26)=1$ condition enforces one course earlier.

## The design principles

Shannon named them in 1949 and every block cipher since is an attempt to get both cheaply:

- **Confusion**: the relationship between key and ciphertext is complicated. Delivered by
  substitution, the S-box, a deliberately non-linear map.
- **Diffusion**: changing one plaintext bit changes about half the ciphertext bits. Delivered by
  permutation and mixing, the [[Transposition Cipher]] idea applied to bits.

Neither is enough alone. A purely linear cipher, however many rounds, collapses to a single linear
map and falls to linear algebra: solve the system and you have the key. That is why the S-box is
the only non-linear part of [[AES]] and why it is the part built on [[Finite Field]] inversion.
Rounds are how you get diffusion to reach the whole block: one round mixes locally, ten rounds mix
everything.

## Core facts

- Symmetric means **the same key both ways**, not that encryption and decryption are the same
  operation (though in a [[Feistel Network]] they very nearly are).
- Symmetric ciphers are roughly $10^3$ times faster than public-key ones per byte. That ratio is
  the reason for hybrid encryption, not a detail.
- Key length is the security parameter: 128-bit [[AES]] means the best known attack is
  brute force at $2^{128}$. DES's 56 bits was broken in public in 1998 and is dead.
- **A symmetric cipher gives confidentiality and nothing else.** It does not tell you who sent the
  message or whether it was altered in transit; [[HMAC]] and [[Digital Signature]] are what do
  that, and assuming otherwise is a real and common bug.
- Kerckhoffs's principle applies: the algorithm is public, the key is not. AES was chosen by open
  competition precisely so it could be attacked in public first.
